title: Corporate Financial Education for Founders
description: Remove the mystery of corporate finance: learn the language, read and interpret your company's financial reports, and use that information to run — and fund — your business with confidence.

lessons.title: Why You Need to Understand Your Company's Financial Information
How to Read Your Company's Financial Reports

quiz.question: Which three reports make up the “Magic Three”?
options: Balance Sheet, Profit & Loss Statement, and Statement of Cash Flows
Budget, Sales Forecast, and Tax Return
Invoice Ledger, Payroll Report, and Bank Statement
Income Projection, Expense Log, and Receipt Book
quiz.explanation: The Balance Sheet, Profit & Loss Statement, and Statement of Cash Flows work together to illuminate the true health of your company.

quiz.question: At its core, corporate finance is about:
options: Filing your company's taxes correctly
Getting the money your company needs and managing it effectively
Choosing the right bank
Setting the prices of your products
quiz.explanation: Every company needs money to operate and generate revenue — corporate finance is the key to getting that money and managing it effectively.

quiz.question: Why do your company's financial reports matter for decision-making?
options: They provide evidence, so you know for certain how your business operates rather than having an idea
They are only needed when applying for loans
They replace the need for a business plan
They are mainly for impressing customers
quiz.explanation: Financial reports provide the evidence that supports your decisions — knowing for certain versus having an idea of the current state of your company.

quiz.question: The Balance Sheet formula is: Assets − Liabilities = ___
options: Net Profit
Working Capital
Equities
Gross Revenue
quiz.explanation: Assets − Liabilities = Equities: what the owners get after all liabilities have been satisfied.

quiz.question: Which section of the Statement of Cash Flows shows how much cash came from founders, investors, and loans?
options: Operating Activities
Investing Activities
Financing Activities
Revenue Activities
quiz.explanation: Financing Activities covers cash from founders and investors, loans and lines of credit, principal paydowns, and distributions.

lessons.title: What Your Balance Sheet Tells You About Your Business
What Your Profit & Loss Statement Tells You About Your Operations
What Your Statement of Cash Flows Tells You About Your Liquidity

quiz.question: Working Capital equals:
options: Total Assets − Total Liabilities
Current Assets − Current Liabilities
Total Revenue − Total Expenses
Cash + Inventory
quiz.explanation: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities — the money available to pay for the operations of the company.

quiz.question: Under the cash basis of accounting, revenue is counted when:
options: It is earned, even if no cash has been received yet
It is earned and the cash is received
The invoice is sent to the customer
The fiscal year closes
quiz.explanation: Cash basis considers revenue when it is earned and cash is received; accrual basis counts it when earned, whether or not cash has arrived.

quiz.question: Your company reaches breakeven when:
options: Total Revenue = Total Expenses
Cash in the bank equals monthly payroll
Gross Revenue = Cost of Goods Sold
Accounts Receivable = Accounts Payable
quiz.explanation: Breakeven is achieved when Total Revenue = Total Expenses, where Total Expenses = Fixed Cost + Variable Cost.

quiz.question: Advertising, delivery, and general & administrative costs belong to which component of the Cost of Operations?
options: Cost of Goods Sold
Operating Expenses
Capital Expenditures
Financing Activities
quiz.explanation: Operating Expenses are the indirect costs — selling expenses, advertising, delivery, G&A, indirect labor. Cost of Goods Sold covers the direct costs of producing the product.

quiz.question: One customer generates the lion's share of your revenue. What does the course say you should do?
options: Celebrate — a big anchor customer means the business is safe
Know what it costs to serve them, because they may be less profitable than they appear — and losing them puts the business at risk
Immediately drop smaller customers to focus on the big one
Raise prices only for the small customers
quiz.explanation: Major customers can cost more than they're worth — and if you lose that customer, your business is at risk. Knowing the cost to service them versus small customers tells you which is truly more profitable.

lessons.title: Projections: Managing Operations and Raising Funds
What a Budget Is and How It Works

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four key projections the course recommends?
options: Sales Projection
12-Month Balance Sheet Projection
Competitor Revenue Projection
Cash Flows Projection
quiz.explanation: The four key projections are the sales projection, 12-month balance sheet projection, expense budget, and cash flows projection.

quiz.question: The best starting point for a realistic, reliable projection is:
options: Your gut feel for where the market is going
Historical data from your own reports, combined with current external information
Copying a template from a similar company
Last year's numbers increased by 10%
quiz.explanation: Start with historical data from your balance sheet, P&L, and cash flows statement, then predict future outcomes using current external information about customers, vendors, and industry trends.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a flexible budget from a static one?
options: It can be altered and adapted throughout the duration of the budget
It only covers variable costs
It is created by outside accountants
It does not require assumptions
quiz.explanation: A static budget does not change for its entire duration; a flexible budget can be altered and adapted along the way.

quiz.question: How often should projections be reviewed against actual performance at a minimum?
options: Once every five years
Only when investors ask
At least once or twice per year — and sooner after a major disruption
Every day
quiz.explanation: Review and update projections at least once or twice per year, and more frequently when something major disrupts operations, sales, resources, or management.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a possible fraud red flag when comparing budget to actual?
options: Payroll increasing without any new staff being hired
Revenue growing faster than expenses
A vendor offering a volume discount
Cash reserves growing alongside profits
quiz.explanation: Increasing payroll without hiring new staff is one of the classic red flags — along with unidentified vendors, duplicate payments, inventory shortfalls, and shrinking cash despite profitable reports.

modules.title: Module 4 — Structuring Your Company's Equity Offering

quiz.question: Who is first in line to receive dividends and other payments?
options: Common stock shareholders
Preferred stock shareholders
General partners
Employees with stock options
quiz.explanation: Preferred stock shares are first to receive dividends and other payments; common stock shares are last.

quiz.question: A limited partnership unit means:
options: Full responsibility for managing the company
No management responsibility, with risk limited to the capital invested
A guaranteed annual dividend
The right to veto company decisions
quiz.explanation: Limited partners have no management responsibility and their risk is limited to the capital they invested. General partners manage the company and bear the most risk.

quiz.question: A SAFE (Simple Agreement for Future Equity) gives the holder:
options: An immediate ownership stake with voting rights
A fixed interest payment like a loan
The right to purchase equity at a discount or a cap on valuation
A seat on the board of directors
quiz.explanation: Pre- and post-SAFE agreements grant the right to purchase equity at a discount or with a cap on valuation — not immediate ownership.

quiz.question: Which of these is a genuine advantage of financing through equity rather than debt?
options: You keep full control of the company
There's no need to pay the money back right away
It guarantees a higher valuation
It has no effect on future returns
quiz.explanation: The biggest benefit of equity financing is that you don't have to pay it back right away — the trade-off is giving up some control and a share of future returns.

modules.title: Module 5 — Interpreting Your Company's Performance Analytics

lessons.title: Ratios and Analytics from the "Magic Three" Reports

quiz.question: Operating Margin is calculated as:
options: Net Sales ÷ Operating Income
Operating Income ÷ Net Sales
Total Revenue ÷ Total Assets
Gross Profit ÷ Total Liabilities
quiz.explanation: Operating Margin = Operating Income ÷ Net Sales. Higher is generally better — the company is efficient at turning sales into profits.

quiz.question: A high accounts receivable turnover ratio suggests:
options: The company is slow to collect what customers owe
Collections are efficient and customers pay their debts quickly
The company has too much inventory
Credit sales should be eliminated
quiz.explanation: A high receivables turnover may indicate efficient collection and a high proportion of quality customers who pay quickly.

quiz.question: The Debt to Equity ratio tells you:
options: How profitable each product line is
The degree to which the company finances its operations through debt versus wholly owned funds
How quickly inventory sells
The company's tax obligation
quiz.explanation: Debt to Equity = Total Liabilities ÷ Total Shareholders' Equity — it reflects whether shareholder equity could cover outstanding debts in a downturn.

quiz.question: A Total Debt to Total Assets ratio greater than 1 means:
options: The company has more assets than liabilities
A considerable portion of assets are funded by debt — the company has more liabilities than assets
The company cannot legally borrow more
Shareholders are guaranteed a dividend
quiz.explanation: A ratio above 1 shows more liabilities than assets — and heightened risk of default if interest rates rise suddenly.

modules.title: Module 6 — Talking About Your Company's Financials

lessons.title: Financial Storytelling and Presenting to Banks and Investors

quiz.question: What are banks fundamentally looking for when they fund a company?
options: A chance at a huge return if the company takes off
A safe return on the money loaned — stability and steady financials
An equity stake in the business
A seat on the board
quiz.explanation: For banks, funding is not an investment — they want a safe return, stability, at least ~3 years of steady financials, and confidence the loan can be serviced.

quiz.question: “THE ASK” in your financial story should cover:
options: How much you need, the structure of the offer (equity or debt), and the next step
Your life story and hobbies
A list of competitors and their weaknesses
Only the size of the market
quiz.explanation: The ask is specific: how much you need, whether the offer is equity or debt, and what the next step is.

quiz.question: Before pitching an investor, the course says you should first:
options: Send the same deck to as many investors as possible
Do your homework on who they are, how they like to be approached, and their funding criteria — then confirm you're a fit
Ask them for a valuation up front
Wait for them to contact you
quiz.explanation: Research who they are, how they prefer to be solicited, and their funding criteria — then customize your pitch to show you're a match.

quiz.question: In “Getting to Yes,” the opportunity is:
options: The big picture of what's possible
What's in it for them — the investors and bankers
The invitation to a follow-up meeting
Your company's origin story
quiz.explanation: Possibility is the big picture; opportunity is what's in it for them; then comes the invitation to take the next step toward “Yes.”
